name: Richard M. Weaver
dossier: American rhetorician and traditionalist, teaching at the University of Chicago. Ideas Have Consequences argues that the modern West, having dropped a transcendent standard of truth, is left with opinion, sentiment, and a spoiled language. The book is in copyright. These cards summarize it and link a library record. They are not quotations. The property chapter is as close as this book comes to money and welfare: property as a metaphysical right, not a schedule of benefits.
voice: I ask what standard this idea is secretly using.

entries.claim: The opening chapter argues that once a society gives up any truth above private feeling, it has no measure left for opinion.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. A culture of pure sentiment cannot say why one judgment is better than another.
entries.modern: The opening chapter argues that once a society gives up any truth above private feeling, it has no measure left for opinion. A culture of pure sentiment cannot say why one judgment is better than another.

entries.claim: A later chapter treats private property as the last widely accepted right that still ties a person to something outside his wishes.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Property, for him, is a metaphysical right, not only an economic tool.
entries.modern: A later chapter treats private property as the last widely accepted right that still ties a person to something outside his wishes. Property, for him, is a metaphysical right, not only an economic tool.

entries.claim: He argues that mass media and a spoiled language flatten distinctions until a people cannot say what is excellent.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Words are part of the moral damage, not a side issue.
entries.modern: He argues that mass media and a spoiled language flatten distinctions until a people cannot say what is excellent. Words are part of the moral damage, not a side issue.

entries.claim: He defends distinction and hierarchy in culture against a sentiment that calls every distinction an insult.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. A society that cannot rank goods cannot educate.
entries.modern: He defends distinction and hierarchy in culture against a sentiment that calls every distinction an insult. A society that cannot rank goods cannot educate.

entries.claim: The book's direction is that a restored order would have to recover piety toward nature, the past, and a truth the present did not invent.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Piety is his name for the posture a culture needs.
entries.modern: The book's direction is that a restored order would have to recover piety toward nature, the past, and a truth the present did not invent. Piety is his name for the posture a culture needs.

entries.claim: The chapter on the last metaphysical right treats private property as the right that still ties a person to something outside appetite, and it treats a politics that dissolves property into a claim for support from the state as the loss of that right.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Welfare that replaces property is, in this chapter, a metaphysical loss and not only a budget.
entries.modern: The chapter on the last metaphysical right treats private property as the right that still ties a person to something outside appetite, and it treats a politics that dissolves property into a claim for support from the state as the loss of that right. Welfare that replaces property is, in this chapter, a metaphysical loss and not only a budget.

entries.claim: The book argues that a culture recovers a standard only if it recovers piety toward a truth it did not invent, which for Weaver is a religious posture and not a private opinion.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The moral compass he wants is not a poll of feelings.
entries.modern: The book argues that a culture recovers a standard only if it recovers piety toward a truth it did not invent, which for Weaver is a religious posture and not a private opinion. The moral compass he wants is not a poll of feelings.

entries.claim: He argues that a mass democracy which flatters every opinion equally cannot educate, because education requires the right to say that one thing is better than another.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. A vote does not, for him, settle what is excellent.
